### Reduced model simulation of non-spatial mapping

#### Connectivity

We included five groups of neurons in this simulation: S1, S2, M1, M2, and B. S1 and S2 represented sensory ensembles, each composed of NS neurons; and M1 and M2 represented motor ensembles, each composed of NM neurons. B represented a ‘switchboard’ ensembles of neurons, akin to Swan and Wyble’s ‘binding pool’ (Swan and Wyble, 2014), comprising NB neurons. Each motor ensemble, with connection weight wMM.

NBS randomly selected switchboard received connections from S1, and another potentially overlapping NBS randomly selected switchboard neurons received connections from S2. If a switchboard neuron was included in the group receiving connections from S1, nBS neurons from S1 were selected to send connections to that switchboard neuron; similarly for S2. Sensory-to-switchboard connections had synaptic weights wBS.

NMB randomly selected switchboard neurons sent connections to M1, and another potentially overlapping NMB randomly selected switchboard neurons sent connections to M2. If a switchboard neuron was included in the group sending connections to M1, nMB neurons in M1 were selected to receive connections from that switchboard neuron; similarly for M2. Switchboard-to-motor connections had synaptic weight wMB.

There were no recurrent connections within either sensory ensemble or within the switchboard ensemble. These connections were omitted since our goal was to demonstrate a proof-of-concept nonspatial-mapping computation through LTP-IE. Exploring the effects of sensory and switchboard recurrence in a more biophysically accurate model may yield fruitful insights into LTP-IE-based computations, however.

#### LTP-IE profile

To encode the mapping (S1→M1, S2→M2) we assigned an LTP-IE value of σ = 2 to all switchboard neurons that either (1) received connections from S1 and sent connections to M1 or (2) received connections from S2 and sent connections to M2. All other neurons were assigned an LTP-IE value of σ = 1. To encode the mapping (S1→M2, S2→M1) we assigned an LTP-IE value of σ = 2 to all switchboard neurons that either (1) received connections from S1 and sent connections to M2 or (2) received connections from S2 and sent connections to M1. All other neurons were assigned an LTP-IE value of σ = 1.

#### Trigger

We triggered recall of an association encoded in the switchboard LTP-IE profile by injecting an external current pulse at timestep two into all the neurons in either S1 or all the neurons in S2.

Summary:

This manuscript investigates, via computer simulations, the functional consequences of a physiological phenomenon known as long-term potentiation of intrinsic excitability (LTP-IE), whereby neurons that fire intensely (due to input S) for a short period of time then respond more strongly to subsequent input (from a different source G). This mechanism is important for several reasons: 1) reports of LTP-IE show a two-fold magnitude increase in EPSPs, substantially higher than what is reported for STDP, and 2) as the authors demonstrate, it can quickly generate highly effective, transient communication channels that may mediate cognitive flexibility. The computer simulations show that this mechanism can explain the replay of place cell responses observed in the hippocampus; specifically, the fact that such activation sequences can replay in forward or reverse order, and over a compressed time scale. More generally, this mechanism is also shown to allow the reactivation of arbitrary response sequences for cells embedded within a recurrent network.

The introduction of intrinsic plasticity concepts to the analysis of population sequences is highly innovative and quite interesting. Although the model has limitations, it represents a feasible and simple mechanism that could underlie hippocampal replay events, and it has other, more general implications. The manuscript is interesting, even provocative, and will certainly enrich the field.

Essential revisions:

The paper requires some updates with regard to the discussion of previous findings by other labs, and some clarification to maximize its impact.

1) Is LTP-IE-time-restricted in the model, or is it assumed to be long-lasting? This is an important question for two reasons. First, because of intersecting trajectories, which could substantially limit the proposed model. The model proficiently generates simple trajectories, such as ABCDE…, but in naturalistic environments (such as open field) there is replay of complex sequences, such as ABCDAEFG. Second, a similar issue arises when the trajectory inducing LTP-IE is very long, as this model would facilitate replays of any length.

The authors should consider some evidence showing that LTP-IE might be time-limited, see e.g. Pignatelli et al., 2019, which would reduce the impact of both of these concerns.

2) Explaining the replay of complex sequences, as mentioned above, would be a major contribution to the field, but it is not clear whether the model can generate those or not. There are many proposed models of reactivation of simple sequences, but none (as far as I know) for reactivation of complex/realistic sequences. While the authors are commended for proposing a new biophysical mechanism for explaining replay, this a moderate contribution to the field. What would be really exciting would be a model such as the one they propose that goes beyond the kind of simple sequences typically found in hippocampus studies with rodents running on linear tracks.

3) Discussion, last paragraph and elsewhere: the authors clearly state that their model works in the absence of synaptic modification, in fact this is one of the major points. This idea (that intrinsic plasticity can act based on existing, but not changing synaptic connectivity) has been presented by other groups before and this prior work should be cited and discussed in appropriate detail.

For instance, previous modeling work (Salinas, 2004; Salinas, 2004) showed that changes in excitability very similar to those proposed here, in which one input modulates the response to another, are ideal for switching a network from one functional configuration (say, sensory-motor map 1) to another (say, sensory-motor map 2). Although the changes in excitability in that earlier work went by a different name, "gain modulation", the underlying mathematics would still apply, so discussing those earlier findings would bolster the argument that LTP-IE could indeed be computationally effective for the sorts of remapping proposed in this manuscript.

The work also needs to be discussed in the context of Moshe Abeles' neuronal avalanche concept (despite its stronger focus on the neocortex).

In the context of LTP-IE, it might be interesting to discuss a recent finding that spike firing can be independent of dendritic EPSP amplitudes, and is instead intrinsically controlled, see Ohtsuki and Hansel, 2018.

4) The authors state that 'this mechanism….is observed in hippocampus only'. If this statement refers to LTP-IE, it is not correct, see e.g. Daoudal, Hanada and Debanne, 2002. Debanne's work should also be cited with regard to STDP. If the statement does not refer to LTP-IE, this needs to be stated more precisely.

5) Given the co-occurrence of replay and sharp-wave ripples, the lack of inhibition in the current model may be a substantial limitation. Replay was triggered using depolarizing current, however the physiological relevance of the model would be bolstered if replay could be triggered by a sharp-wave ripple event in an inhibitory population. More broadly, how does the model behave if one were to add inhibition in addition to excitation?

6) Related to the above point, it was difficult to evaluate the robustness of the model. There are many parameters, but which ones are more critical for the results, and what is the 'operating range' of the model? Is the model robust to small perturbations in parameters?

7) Regarding Figure 4, it is unclear where in the brain a recurrent sensorimotor network with LTP-IE might exist to support the generation of transient associations using the proposed mechanism. What do the authors suggest is the biophysical substrate for non-spatial transient associations?

8) Some parts of the manuscript were found to be somewhat technical and difficult to follow. Specifically, throughout the Results: second paragraph; subsection “LTPIE increases membrane voltages and spike rates under random gating inputs”, first and last paragraphs; subsection “Spike sequences propagate along LTP-IE-defined paths through a network”, second paragraph; subsection “Dependence of LTP-IE-based sequence propagation on network parameters”, first paragraph and subsection “LTP-IE-based sequences can encode temporary stimulus response mappings”, last paragraph. The Results should be more accessible to a broader readership not specialized in computational neuroscience.

For instance, it is not easy to understand how the results in Figure 2 relate to, and emerge from, those in Figure 1. In general, it would be useful if the authors could better explain the relationship between their neuronal mechanism and the results.

In addition, while the model works well for encoding spatial trajectories in which the closeness of individual locations is pre-encoded in the recurrent connectivity weights, it is difficult to see how this would extend to the given example of cognitive flexibility (i.e., raising our right hand when a particular word is heard, and the left hand when a different word is heard), particularly if no a priori spatial relationship exists. Are spatial relationships necessary? There is no evidence provided to suggest that the neocortical network has the necessary architecture to support LTP-IE based replay.

claims.claim: Even in a randomly connected network with no spatial structure, LTP-IE can yield selective stimulus-response mappings.
claims.source: Thus, even in a randomly connected network with no spatial structure, LTP-IE can yield selective stimulus-response mappings, demonstrating the potential of excitability changes as a substrate for cognitive flexibility more generally.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the reduced model results.

claims.claim: Sequence replay has been observed in vivo in both hippocampus and cortex during awake quiescent periods in both rodents and primates.
claims.source: One noteworthy empirical example of internally generated sequences is the replay of spike sequences representing an animal's recent sensorimotor sequence, such as a locomotor trajectory or sequence of viewed images. Sequence replay has been observed in vivo in both hippocampus and cortex during awake quiescent periods in both rodents and primates (Foster and Wilson, 2006; Davidson et al., 2009; Karlsson and Frank, 2009; Gupta et al., 2010; Carr et al., 2011; Eagleman and Dragoi, 2012) and is thought to be involved in memory consolidation (Carr et al., 2011; Jadhav et al., 2012; Ólafsdóttir et al., 2017; Zielinski et al., 2017) and navigational planning (Foster and Knierim, 2012; Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental citations.

claims.claim: Replay is thought to be involved in memory consolidation and navigational planning.
claims.source: Sequence replay has been observed in vivo in both hippocampus and cortex during awake quiescent periods in both rodents and primates (Foster and Wilson, 2006; Davidson et al., 2009; Karlsson and Frank, 2009; Gupta et al., 2010; Carr et al., 2011; Eagleman and Dragoi, 2012) and is thought to be involved in memory consolidation (Carr et al., 2011; Jadhav et al., 2012; Ólafsdóttir et al., 2017; Zielinski et al., 2017) and navigational planning (Foster and Knierim, 2012; Pfeiffer and Foster, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claims.claim: LTP-IE biases recently active cells towards recruitment during replay, with their reactivation order determined by pre-existing but fixed recurrent connectivity.
claims.source: Briefly, LTP-IE biases recently active cells towards recruitment during replay, with their reactivation order determined by pre-existing but fixed recurrent connectivity.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the model mechanism.

claims.claim: The potentiated pathways in the network supported stable and self-sustaining spike sequences.
claims.source: Similar to 'synfire chains', feedforward neural networks supporting stable activity propagation (Abeles, 1982; Abeles et al., 1994; Herrmann et al., 1995; Schrader et al., 2008), the potentiated pathways in our network supported stable and self-sustaining spike sequences, which despite symmetric connectivity propagated without reversing direction due to the moderate refractory period we included (8 ms).
claims.evidence: This is a description of model behavior compared to synfire chains.

claims.claim: Despite symmetric connectivity, sequences propagated without reversing direction due to the moderate refractory period.
claims.source: Similar to 'synfire chains', feedforward neural networks supporting stable activity propagation (Abeles, 1982; Abeles et al., 1994; Herrmann et al., 1995; Schrader et al., 2008), the potentiated pathways in our network supported stable and self-sustaining spike sequences, which despite symmetric connectivity propagated without reversing direction due to the moderate refractory period we included (8 ms).
claims.evidence: This is an explanation of model behavior.

claims.claim: The spatial network can be conceptualized as akin to a reservoir of trajectories through space that can be selected for replay in an experience-dependent manner through LTP-IE.
claims.source: One can therefore conceptualize our spatial network as akin to a reservoir of trajectories through space that can be selected for replay in an experience-dependent manner through LTP-IE.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the model's computational function.

claims.claim: Despite substantial variability in the membrane voltages of LTP-IE-tagged cells and overlap with non-LTP-IE-tagged cells, replay events exhibited stable propagation along LTP-IE-defined network paths, due to averaging effects of populations of LTP-IE-tagged cells.
claims.source: First, despite substantial variability in the membrane voltages of LTP-IE-tagged cells and overlap with non-LTP-IE-tagged cells (Figure 1D), replay events exhibited stable propagation along LTP-IE-defined network paths, due to averaging effects of populations of LTP-IE-tagged cells.
claims.evidence: This is an observation about model robustness.

claims.claim: Sequences replayed at timescales determined by the network rather than the original trajectory.
claims.source: Second, sequences replayed at timescales determined by the network rather than the original trajectory (Figure 3F), and did so in both forward and reverse (Figure 2F,G), capturing these two key empirical features of hippocampal replay (Foster and Wilson, 2006; Davidson et al., 2009; Karlsson and Frank, 2009; Gupta et al., 2010; Carr et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in the model and compared to experimental observations.

claims.claim: Inhibition played an important role in promoting replay in one direction only.
claims.source: Additionally, inhibition played an important role in our model, promoting replay in one direction only (Figure 2F) and inducing competition among multiple sequences in branched trajectories (Figure 3D,I,J), even though inhibition bore no spatial organization itself.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in the model results.

claims.claim: Inhibition induced competition among multiple sequences in branched trajectories.
claims.source: Additionally, inhibition played an important role in our model, promoting replay in one direction only (Figure 2F) and inducing competition among multiple sequences in branched trajectories (Figure 3D,I,J), even though inhibition bore no spatial organization itself.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in the model results.

claims.claim: The SWR events in the model were consistent with the observation that hippocampal SWRs likely arise spontaneously in CA3 and propagate to CA1.
claims.source: Inhibition also appeared to shape the power spectra of the sharp-wave-ripple (SWR) events in our model arising in the PC population average alongside replayed sequences; moreover, these events were consistent with the observation that hippocampal SWRs likely arise spontaneously in CA3 and propagate to CA1 (Buzsáki, 1986; Csicsvari et al., 2000; Carr et al., 2011; Ramirez-Villegas et al., 2018), since our model's excitatory recurrence was inspired by that found in CA3 but not CA1 (Lisman, 1999).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of model behavior to experimental observations.

claims.claim: LTP-IE might also occur purely intrinsically, without an explicit correlation with EPSP sizes.
claims.source: For instance, LTP-IE might also occur purely intrinsically, without an explicit correlation with EPSP sizes (Ohtsuki and Hansel, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on a citation to another study.

claims.claim: LTP-IE-like phenomena have been observed in cortex.
claims.source: This latter example may be relevant to excitability-based computations in cortex, where LTP-IE-like phenomena have been observed (Sourdet et al., 2003; Paz, 2009), but whose internal network structures do not necessarily exhibit clear spatial organization.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claims.claim: Preferential connectivity among similarly tuned cells has been observed in mouse visual cortex.
claims.source: We note, however, that preferential connectivity among similarly tuned cells has been observed in mouse visual cortex (Ko et al., 2011), suggesting a mechanism similar to the one we have explored might support spontaneous sequence propagation among neurons encoding visual space.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to an experimental study.

claims.claim: History-dependent excitability changes might occur over slower timescales as well.
claims.source: History-dependent excitability changes might also occur not just at the rapid timescales that have motivated our work but over slower timescales as well (Zhang and Linden, 2003; Titley et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to other studies.

claims.claim: Small neuronal ensembles could be 'imprinted' into a mouse cortical network and subsequently reactivated in vivo via repeated optogenetic stimulation.
claims.source: For example, it was recently found that small neuronal ensembles could be 'imprinted' into a mouse cortical network and subsequently reactivated in vivo via repeated optogenetic stimulation (Carrillo-Reid et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to an experimental study.

claims.claim: The result from Carrillo-Reid et al. (2016) could arise via increasing neural excitabilities instead of Hebbian plasticity.
claims.source: While this result was suggested to provide evidence of Hebbian (homosynaptic) plasticity, our work suggests that the same result could arise via increasing neural excitabilities instead.
claims.evidence: This is a reinterpretation of experimental results based on the current model.

claims.claim: Excitability changes alone might quickly and selectively reshape network dynamics.
claims.source: Overall, our work demonstrates how excitability changes alone might quickly and selectively reshape network dynamics, implicating their potential role in storing memories and encoding stimulus-response mappings, and more generally in organizing flexible computations over rapid timescales.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the work.

claims.claim: Oscillation-based models for encoding and decoding sequences in hippocampus suppose that sequential information is stored in the timing of spikes relative to theta and gamma oscillatory cycles.
claims.source: One family of models for encoding and decoding sequences in hippocampus supposes that sequential information is stored in the timing of spikes relative to theta (4–8 Hz) and gamma (~40 Hz) oscillatory cycles in the hippocampus (Lisman and Idiart, 1995; Lisman, 1999).
claims.evidence: This is a description of prior models based on citations.

claims.claim: It is not clear how sensory input would be appropriately transformed to be 'entered' into the oscillation cycle at the correct time in oscillation-based models.
claims.source: While these models provide a persuasive computational account of how oscillations might be used to store temporary information, it is not clear how the sensory input would be appropriately transformed so as to be 'entered' into the oscillation cycle at the correct time, how stable these mechanisms are in the face of noise, nor how multiple sequences might be stored simultaneously; in particular, sequence information could be lost if the oscillation were disrupted, and one would require an independent nested oscillation for a second sequence.
claims.evidence: This is a critique of oscillation-based models.

claims.claim: In the LTP-IE-based model, memories are directly entered into the network by physiological spiking patterns.
claims.source: In our LTP-IE-based spiking-network model, however, memories are directly entered into the network by physiological spiking patterns (Figure 1), are stored in effective synaptic weight changes likely driven by ion channel inactivation (as opposed to persistent spiking activity) and might therefore be more robust to noise, and multiple sequences can theoretically be stored in the same network in a manner similar to how we have stored multiple stimulus-response mappings in Figure 4.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of the current model to oscillation-based models.

claims.claim: The second main family of replay models assumes sequences are initially induced via modification of recurrent network weights through mechanisms like STDP.
claims.source: The second main family of replay models either explicitly (Molter et al., 2007; Veliz-Cuba et al., 2015; Haga and Fukai, 2018) or implicitly (Chenkov et al., 2017) assumes the sequences produced by the network are initially induced in the network via modification of recurrent network weights, for example through homosynaptic mechanisms like spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) (Markram et al., 1997; Bi and Poo, 1998; Fiete et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is a description of prior models based on citations.

claims.claim: It is unclear whether STDP-based mechanisms could account for awake trajectory replay that can occur after a single trajectory experience.
claims.source: While such models can indeed selectively bias network sequences, given the hypothesized weak magnitude of STDP, it is unclear whether such a mechanism could account for the awake trajectory replay observed in rodents, which can sometimes occur even when the animal has experienced the original trajectory only once (Foster and Wilson, 2006), nor whether it could be used to immediately induce novel computations that the animal cannot afford to learn over extensive repetitions.
claims.evidence: This is a critique of STDP-based models based on experimental observations.

claims.claim: In the LTP-IE model, LTP-IE 'tags' cells in the recurrent network with a higher probability of spiking in response to input, and sequential ordering is reconstructed by the existing but unmodified recurrent connectivity.
claims.source: In our model we rely on a strong, fast-acting mechanism, LTP-IE, which although heterosynaptic (unlike STDP, LTP-IE follows spiking regardless of which input elicited the spikes [Hyun et al., 2013; Hyun et al., 2015) suffices in biasing a network toward producing highly specific sequences: LTP-IE 'tags' cells in the recurrent network with a higher probability of spiking in response to input (Figure 1), and sequential ordering is reconstructed by the existing but unmodified recurrent connectivity.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of the current model to STDP-based models.

claims.claim: Experience-dependent short-term plasticity mechanisms, like lingering presynaptic calcium, can transiently make a neural ensemble more sensitive to subsequent inputs.
claims.source: We would also like to note that experience-dependent short-term plasticity mechanisms, like lingering presynaptic calcium following spiking, can transiently make a neural ensemble more sensitive to subsequent inputs (Mongillo et al., 2008), suggesting such a mechanism might be able to play a similar role to excitability changes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to another study.

claims.claim: Changes in how dendrites integrate EPSPs to trigger spiking can co-occur with canonical STDP or LTP.
claims.source: For instance, it has been observed that changes in how dendrites integrate EPSPs to trigger spiking (effectively an excitability change since this would affect spiking even if EPSPs remained stable) can co-occur with canonical STDP or LTP (Daoudal et al., 2002; Daoudal and Debanne, 2003; Campanac and Debanne, 2008; Debanne and Poo, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claims.claim: Replaying place-tuned firing sequences in vitro that were previously recorded in vivo could induce long-term connectivity changes between cells with overlapping place fields.
claims.source: Indeed, it was shown that replaying place-tuned firing sequences in vitro that were previously recorded in vivo could induce long-term connectivity changes between cells with overlapping place fields (Isaac et al., 2009, J. Neurosci.).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to an experimental study.

claims.claim: LTP-IE may serve as a temporary buffer for sequences that could become embedded in the network as long-term memories through gradual synaptic changes triggered by repeated replay.
claims.source: Thus, LTP-IE may serve as a temporary buffer for sequences that could become embedded in the network as long-term memories through gradual synaptic changes triggered by repeated replay.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the functional role of LTP-IE.

claims.claim: LTP-IE-based replay in the model occurred over a wide range of parameters.
claims.source: Additionally, LTP-IE-based replay in our model occurred over a wide range of parameters.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in the parameter sweeps.

claims.claim: Paths defined by pre-existing stronger connections should bias replay in their favor but might also be overwritten by transient excitability changes encoding paths just traveled.
claims.source: Intuitively, paths defined by pre-existing stronger connections should bias replay in their favor but might also be overwritten by transient excitability changes encoding paths just traveled.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about how LTP-IE might interact with heterogeneous connectivity.

claims.claim: Short-term memory and computational flexibility and their subsequent effect on memory consolidation and long-term network structure likely rely on a host of dynamics and plasticity mechanisms.
claims.source: Overall, short-term memory and computational flexibility and their subsequent effect on memory consolidation and long-term network structure likely rely on a host of dynamics and plasticity mechanisms, but we propose LTP-IE may play a significant role.
claims.evidence: This is a concluding statement about the role of LTP-IE.

claims.claim: Selectively biasing cell recruitment without changing recurrence generalizes beyond increasing spike responses through LTP-IE.
claims.source: Finally, selectively biasing cell recruitment without changing recurrence generalizes beyond increasing spike responses through LTP-IE.
claims.evidence: This introduces a broader principle.

claims.claim: Differential baseline inputs can act as context signals and control the gain of sensory signals without affecting their tuning.
claims.source: Such differential baseline inputs can act as context signals, and if interacting multiplicatively with sensory signals can control the gain of the latter without affecting their tuning; by modulating the gain of different neurons in such a way, one can then selectively and transiently encode context-dependent sensorimotor mappings without modifying synaptic weights (Salinas, 2004b; Salinas, 2004a), similar to how one might do so with LTP-IE.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Neurons in entorhinal cortex have been shown to support history-dependent, graded persistent activity.
claims.source: Indeed, neurons in entorhinal cortex, which inspired the gating signals G in our network, have been shown to support history-dependent, graded persistent activity (Egorov et al., 2002), suggesting the recurrent CA3 network could be subject to differential baseline inputs maintained over short-term memory timescales.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to an experimental study.

claims.claim: Differential baseline inputs could act in concert with LTP-IE as an additional rapid and controllable gating signal.
claims.source: Such a mechanism could act in concert with LTP-IE and could potentially act as an additional rapid and controllable gating signal governing effective excitabilities of neurons in the recurrent network.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about how different mechanisms might interact.

claims.claim: With no forgetting or selective LTP-IE activation, one would expect all neurons to undergo LTP-IE after the animal had fully explored the environment.
claims.source: Indeed, with no forgetting or selective LTP-IE activation, one would expect all neurons in our model to undergo LTP-IE after the animal had fully explored the environment, thus preventing sequential reactivation along specific trajectories through the network.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about model limitations.

claims.claim: The neurotransmitter acetylcholine is known to interact with the voltage-gated potassium channel Kv1.2.
claims.source: For example, the neurotransmitter acetylcholine is known to interact with the voltage-gated potassium channel Kv1.2 (Hattan et al., 2002), the ion channel hypothesized to underlie LTP-IE (Hyun et al., 2015), and hippocampus receives state-dependent cholinergic inputs from medial septum (Yoder and Pang, 2005; Mamad et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claims.claim: Memory-related excitability changes in dentate gyrus have been shown to decay after two hours.
claims.source: Furthermore, memory-related excitability changes in dentate gyrus have been shown to decay after two hours (Pignatelli et al., 2019), suggesting similar decay mechanisms may exist in CA3.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to an experimental study.

claims.claim: Sufficient machinery for erasing or selectively modulating the overall effects of LTP-IE may converge in hippocampus.
claims.source: Thus, sufficient machinery for erasing or selectively modulating the overall effects of LTP-IE, for example as a function of arousal or motivation state, may converge in the brain region that has served as the inspiration for our model.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on the cited mechanisms.

claims.claim: Regulation of the spatiotemporal extent of excitability changes would be crucial in preventing pathological dynamics.
claims.source: Clinically, one would also expect regulation of the spatiotemporal extent of excitability changes to be crucial in preventing pathological dynamics, such as incomplete signal transmission that might lead to short-term memory deficits (Vallar and Shallice, 2007), or hyperexcitability without sufficient compensatory inhibition leading to seizure-like events, as exhibited in the 'blowup' regime of our spiking network model (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about clinical implications.

claims.claim: Cortical activity likely contains higher order structure beyond mean firing rates, such as grid-like representations of space in entorhinal cortex.
claims.source: Additionally, while we have assumed the upstream 'gating' inputs in our model are stochastic with homogeneous firing rates, cortical activity likely contains higher order structure beyond mean firing rates, such as the grid-like representations of space observed in neural firing patterns in entorhinal cortex (O'Keefe and Burgess, 2005; Yamamoto and Tonegawa, 2017), the hippocampal input that inspired our gating inputs G.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claims.claim: The model demonstrates that replay can occur absent additional mnemonic information.
claims.source: Our model demonstrates that replay can occur absent additional mnemonic information, but one would imagine such additional information would only increase the capacity and robustness for memory storage and computational flexibility, since this would act as an additional memory buffer.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion about the model's capabilities.

claims.claim: Entorhinal neurons may have the capacity for history-dependent persistent activity persisting over the same timescales as LTP-IE.
claims.source: Furthermore, as mentioned above, entorhinal neurons may have the capacity for history-dependent persistent activity persisting over the same timescales as LTP-IE (Egorov et al., 2002), potentially supporting even more flexible heterogeneous gating inputs to the recurrent network.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to an experimental study.

claims.claim: Empirical replay events and their accompanying sharp-wave ripples have typically been observed to occur over approximately 100 ms.
claims.source: Indeed, while empirical replay events and their accompanying sharp-wave ripples have typically been observed to occur over approximately 100 ms (Carr et al., 2011), when animals are allowed to explore larger environments replay can last several hundred milliseconds (Davidson et al., 2009), suggesting replay durations might be largely determined by the size of the environment, as in our model.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claims.claim: Hippocampal sequence replay may be gated by particular phases of slow, theta oscillations.
claims.source: Parallel lines of evidence, however, suggest hippocampal sequence replay may be gated by particular phases of slow, theta oscillations (4–8 Hz), which would constrain replay to occur within approximately 100–200 ms time windows (Lisman and Idiart, 1995; Fuentemilla et al., 2010; Lisman, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Spatiotemporal propagation of activity in certain neural networks may follow a power-law distribution.
claims.source: Finally, an intriguing line of research suggests spatiotemporal propagation of activity in certain neural networks may follow a power-law distribution (Beggs and Plenz, 2003; Beggs and Plenz, 2004; Plenz and Thiagarajan, 2007; Fiete et al., 2010; Scarpetta and de Candia, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Activity patterns distributed as power-law would imply scale invariance of activity structures and suggest the network state sits at a phase transition between dynamical regimes.
claims.source: Activity patterns distributed as such would imply scale invariance (scale-freeness) of activity structures and suggest the network state sits at a phase transition between dynamical regimes that may be optimal for processing inputs that vary over a large range (Shew et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is based on citation to prior work.

claims.claim: The model would not be expected to exhibit scale-free activity patterns because activity levels and durations were capped by inhibition and refractoriness, and by the limited environment size.
claims.source: Since activity levels and durations in our network were capped by inhibition and refractoriness, and by the limited environment size, we would not expect our network to exhibit scale-free activity patterns; however, exploring what network mechanisms and connectivity statistics could yield power-law distributed sequences through LTP-IE and examining how these might be involved in sequence-based stimulus processing would be an exciting line of future inquiry.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about model limitations.

claims.claim: Pharmacological blocking of LTP-IE during exploration should prevent the encoding of new trajectory information into CA3, consequently preventing subsequent replay.
claims.source: First, pharmacological blocking of LTP-IE during exploration should prevent the encoding of new trajectory information into CA3, consequently preventing subsequent replay. This could be achieved by in vivo application of nimodipine or PP2, which block intracellular calcium increase, protein tyrosine kinase activation, and Kv1.2 channel endocytosis, all potential mechanisms of LTP-IE, and which have been shown to block LTP-IE in vitro (Hyun et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental prediction based on the model.

claims.claim: Inactivating medial entorhinal layer II should inhibit CA3 sequential replay events.
claims.source: Second, inactivating medial entorhinal layer II (MEC II), which projects to CA3 and which we associate with gating inputs G in our analogy with hippocampal circuitry, should inhibit CA3 sequential replay events. Indeed, inactivation of MEC III inputs has been shown to inhibit forms of replay in CA1 (Yamamoto and Tonegawa, 2017); we propose that a parallel effect would be seen in MEC II inputs to CA3.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental prediction based on the model and prior experimental results.

claims.claim: The core prediction of the sequence induction model is that neurons do not have to be initially activated in the order (or reverse order) in which they will later reactivate.
claims.source: Finally, the core prediction of our sequence induction model is that the neurons do not have to be initially activated in the order (or the reverse order) in which they will later reactivate. As the only information explicitly added to the network at the time of encoding is the set of neurons activated, speed or ordering information must be reconstructed from existing connectivity.
claims.evidence: This is a key prediction of the model mechanism.

claims.claim: The model predicts that replay would occur in an order corresponding to a path through the environment, rather than the order in which virtual places were presented.
claims.source: Our model predicts that as long as the animal had sufficient knowledge of which sensory cues corresponded to which environment locations, replay would occur in an order corresponding to a path through the environment, rather than the order in which the virtual places were presented.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental prediction based on the model.

claims.claim: The model suggests a link between isotropy in pre-existing spatial representations and the observation that replay sometimes occurs in forward and sometimes in reverse order.
claims.source: First, it suggests a link between isotropy in pre-existing spatial representations in the network (i.e. the spatially organized connectivity) and the experimental observation that replay sometimes occurs in the forward, and sometimes in the reverse order relative to the neurons' initial activation during the trajectory (Foster and Wilson, 2006; Davidson et al., 2009; Carr et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is an insight from the model compared to experimental observations.

claims.claim: Since no directionality information is stored by LTP-IE, replay should occur with equal chance in forward or reverse.
claims.source: In particular, since no directionality information is stored by LTP-IE (which only tags which neurons were recently active), replay should occur with equal chance in forward or reverse.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on the model mechanism.

claims.claim: Reverse replay would not be expected for neural sequences that do not have a natural spatial embedding.
claims.source: One would therefore not expect to observe reverse replay for neural sequences that do not have a natural spatial embedding, for example spoken sentences in humans.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on the model mechanism.

claims.claim: The upstream gating signal might serve as a substrate for the short-term state-dependence of replay.
claims.source: Second, the upstream gating signal in our model might serve as a substrate for the short-term state-dependence of replay, for example with arousal or motivation controlling when the gating signal is present or absent.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the model's functional implications.

claims.claim: The gating signal could ensure that replay occurs only at appropriate times without interfering with other computations.
claims.source: This could ensure that replay occurs only at appropriate times (e.g. quiescent rest) without interfering with other computations being performed by the network, such as pattern separation in external sensory inputs (Leutgeb et al., 2007; Bakker et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the functional role of the gating signal.

claims.claim: The 'binding pool' model of associative short-term memory could potentially be recast in the framework of excitability-based information flow.
claims.source: One example of a network model with no obvious spatial embedding, and which could potentially be recast in the framework of excitability-based information flow, is the 'binding pool' model of associative short-term memory proposed by Swan and Wyble (2014).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to another model.

claims.claim: Persistent spiking in coding mnemonic information is presently undergoing substantial reevaluation.
claims.source: While the role of such persistent spiking in coding mnemonic information is presently undergoing substantial reevaluation (Sreenivasan et al., 2014), one could theoretically replace it with excitability increases, with an equivalent consequence for information transmission.
claims.evidence: This is based on citation to a review.

claims.claim: The switchboard/binding pool architecture may be well suited to transiently storing novel mappings through LTP-IE that the network has never seen before.
claims.source: Notably, since connectivity here required no training, this architecture may be well suited to transiently storing novel mappings through LTP-IE that the network has never seen before, so long as the neural ensembles encoding the relevant stimuli and responses were sufficiently (but randomly) connected to the switchboard/binding pool.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the computational capabilities of the model.

claims.claim: External modulatory inputs to a recurrent network could control the speed at which a computation performed by the network unfolded through time.
claims.source: Indeed, it was recently shown that external modulatory inputs to a recurrent network could control the speed at which a computation performed by the network unfolded through time, closely recapitulating experimental results (Remington et al., 2018)
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claims.claim: The control of information flow and computation in recurrent networks via effective excitability alone, without structural connectivity changes, might be a rich framework for investigating rapid cognitive flexibility and short-term information storage.
claims.source: We propose that the control of information flow and computation in recurrent networks via effective excitability alone, without structural connectivity changes, might be a rich framework for investigating rapid cognitive flexibility and short-term information storage.
claims.evidence: This is a concluding proposal about the broader implications of the work.

results.result: The authors implement LTP-IE in a leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron model where neurons receive sensorimotor (S), recurrent (R), and gating (G) inputs. LTP-IE is applied when neurons fire at 10-20 Hz for 1 second, scaling G inputs by a factor σ(r). This increases membrane voltage, variability, and spiking probability in response to inputs, with moderate synaptic weights (wPC,G) enabling spike probability increases from near zero to ~0.5.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C50 collectively describe the LIF model implementation and demonstrate LTP-IE effects on membrane voltage and spiking probability through simulation data shown in Figure 1. The sigmoid activation function choice is justified by experimental data (C45), and the physiological firing rate range (10-20 Hz) matches place cell activity (C50). The model behavior is well-characterized across parameter ranges.

results.result: The model network consists of 3000 pyramidal cells (PCs) with place-field tuning and 300 inhibitory neurons. PCs have recurrent excitatory connections with strength proportional to place field similarity. LTP-IE tags cells along a trajectory but does not store order or timing information. Inhibition limits active PC numbers and prevents bidirectional propagation.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C51 describe the network architecture, which is clearly specified in the methods and demonstrated in Figure 2. The spatial organization, connectivity rules, and inhibitory architecture are well-defined. The claim that order/timing are not stored by LTP-IE (C37) is a key design feature that is subsequently validated by the model's ability to reconstruct sequences from connectivity alone.

results.result: Spontaneous replay events lasting 100-200 ms arise in the network with random gating inputs. Replay propagates in both forward and reverse directions, matching experimental observations. The 8 ms refractory period ensures unidirectional propagation. Replay can handle nonlinear trajectories and is trajectory-specific, not determined by connectivity alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C58 describe the main replay results demonstrated in Figure 2F-I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1. The bidirectional replay (C53) matches cited experimental data. The trajectory-specificity (C56) is demonstrated by showing different trajectories produce different replay patterns. Population firing rates suggest connection to sharp-wave ripples (C58), though this is presented as a potential connection rather than definitive.

results.result: Replay events occur robustly across a wide range of network parameters including excitatory/inhibitory feedback strengths, connectivity length scales, LTP-IE levels, and gating input rates. Replay speed depends on connectivity parameters. Without sufficient inhibition, the network enters a 'blowup' regime or exhibits bidirectional events. Power spectral analysis shows oscillatory activity at tens of Hz, with frequency depending on inhibition strength.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C68 describe parameter sweep results shown in Figure 3A-H. The robustness across parameter ranges is well-demonstrated through systematic variation. The 'blowup' regime (C61) is clearly identified. The SWR-like oscillations (C65) occur at lower frequencies than biological SWRs (C66), but the model suggests this may be tunable through excitatory-inhibitory balance (C68), which is a reasonable inference from the data.

results.result: In branched trajectory simulations, replay events can navigate through intersections, selecting a single path to continue. Without inhibition, sequences propagate along all branches, suggesting inhibition implements winner-take-all dynamics among competing sequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71 describe results from branched trajectory simulations shown in Figure 3I-J. The comparison between networks with and without inhibition (C70) provides clear evidence for the winner-take-all interpretation (C71). This is a logical inference well-supported by the contrasting behaviors.

results.result: Experience-dependent LTP-IE at biological levels can rapidly and selectively modulate sequence propagation through realistic spiking neural networks across a range of parameter regimes.
results.evaluation: Claim C72 is a summary conclusion supported by the collective evidence from parameter sweeps (C59-C68) and the demonstration of sequence propagation (C52-C58). The biological plausibility is established through the use of experimentally-measured LTP-IE parameters and physiological firing rates.

results.result: LTP-IE can induce multiple stimulus-response mappings in the network, with the same mapping implementable through different LTP-IE paths reflected in different response delays. This contrasts with other models that assume unique mapping representations and suggests LTP-IE provides a flexible substrate for temporary mappings.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C78 describe stimulus-response mapping results shown in Figure 4. The demonstration of multiple implementations of the same mapping (C75-C76) is clearly shown. The comparison to other models (C77) is appropriately cited. The conclusion about flexibility (C78) is a reasonable inference from the demonstrated multiplicity of implementations.

results.result: A reduced network model operating in discrete time was developed where LTP-IE-tagged neurons receive twice the background gating input, and inhibition is implemented by limiting maximum simultaneously active neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81 describe the reduced model architecture detailed in the Methods section. This is a straightforward description of the simplified model used for proof-of-concept demonstrations.

results.result: Using the reduced model with multi-dimensional (position and head-direction) tuning, LTP-IE can support replay of self-intersecting trajectories in the correct order without random branching. Random branching probability would increase for less orthogonal intersections.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C84 describe results from the reduced model shown in Figure 5A-C. The successful replay through intersections is demonstrated. The inference about less orthogonal intersections (C84) is reasonable based on the connectivity structure, though not directly tested.

results.result: In a randomly connected network without spatial structure, LTP-IE can encode stimulus-response mappings through selective tagging of 'switchboard' neurons that connect stimulus and motor ensembles. This demonstrates excitability-based computation in non-spatial networks.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C88 describe non-spatial mapping results shown in Figure 5D-E. The demonstration is clear and the comparison to the binding pool model (C87) is appropriately cited. The conclusion about general excitability-based computation (C88) is supported by this proof-of-concept demonstration.

results.result: Hippocampal and cortical replay of spike sequences occurs during rest following exploration, at compressed timescales and often in reverse order. Replay has been implicated in memory consolidation and planning.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C15-C19, C89-C90 describe established experimental observations about neural replay, all supported by multiple citations to experimental literature. These provide the empirical motivation for the modeling work.

results.result: LTP-IE in CA3 pyramidal cells causes EPSPs from medial entorhinal cortex to more than double within 8 seconds following 1-2 seconds of 10-20 Hz spiking. This heterosynaptic mechanism persists for minutes and occurs at physiologically relevant firing rates, suggesting it may occur naturally. LTP-IE has only been observed in hippocampus.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C28 describe the experimental LTP-IE phenomenon from cited studies (Hyun et al. 2013, 2015). The characterization is accurate to the cited work. The inference that it may occur naturally (C25) is reasonable given the firing rate match (C24). The statement about hippocampus-only observation (C28) is a factual statement about current experimental evidence.

results.result: Cognitive flexibility likely depends on modulating network dynamics. Existing mechanisms for inducing stimulus-response mappings require slow modifications through synaptic plasticity. STDP produces small changes and may occur rarely given low cortical firing rates and timing requirements, leading computational models to require many trials over extended periods. Modifying connections risks catastrophic forgetting.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C14 establish the scientific context and motivation. The characterization of STDP limitations (C8-C10) is supported by cited experimental work. The inference about STDP rarity (C10) is reasonable given the cited firing rates and timing requirements. The computational model limitations (C11) and catastrophic forgetting concern (C12) are appropriately cited.

results.result: The model mechanism involves LTP-IE biasing recently active cells toward recruitment during replay, with ordering determined by fixed recurrent connectivity. The network supports stable, self-sustaining sequences that propagate unidirectionally due to refractoriness. Replay occurs at network-determined timescales in both directions. Inhibition promotes unidirectional replay and competition among sequences. The model's SWR-like events are consistent with CA3 origin of hippocampal SWRs.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C99 summarize key model features and their relationship to experimental observations. These are well-supported by the simulation results presented in Figures 2-3. The comparison to synfire chains (C92) and experimental SWR properties (C99) are appropriately contextualized with citations.

results.result: The LTP-IE model is compared to oscillation-based and STDP-based replay models. Oscillation models have unclear input transformation mechanisms and limited multi-sequence capacity. STDP-based models may not account for single-trial replay given weak STDP magnitude. The LTP-IE model uses strong, fast heterosynaptic plasticity to tag cells, with ordering from fixed connectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C113 provide critical comparison to alternative models, appropriately cited. The critiques of oscillation-based (C108) and STDP-based (C111) models are reasonable given the cited limitations. The characterization of the LTP-IE model's advantages (C109, C112) is supported by the demonstrated results. The mention of short-term plasticity (C113) appropriately acknowledges alternative mechanisms.

results.result: Excitability changes may interact with synaptic plasticity mechanisms like STDP/LTP. Replayed sequences compressed in time may trigger STDP, potentially transferring LTP-IE-based temporary memories to long-term synaptic changes. The model's robustness across parameters suggests potential interaction with heterogeneous connectivity. Multiple mechanisms likely contribute to memory and flexibility.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C119 discuss interactions between LTP-IE and synaptic plasticity. The co-occurrence of excitability and synaptic changes (C114) is supported by citations. The speculation about LTP-IE as a temporary buffer (C116) is reasonable given the time compression of replay and STDP timing requirements. The acknowledgment of multiple mechanisms (C119) is appropriately cautious.

results.result: Selectively biasing cell recruitment generalizes beyond LTP-IE to include differential baseline inputs that can act as context signals controlling gain. Entorhinal neurons show history-dependent persistent activity that could provide differential inputs to CA3, potentially acting in concert with LTP-IE.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C123 discuss alternative mechanisms for selective recruitment. The gain modulation mechanism (C121) is appropriately cited. The observation about entorhinal persistent activity (C122) is supported by citation. The speculation about combined mechanisms (C123) is reasonable but clearly presented as speculative.

results.result: Without forgetting or selective activation, all neurons would eventually undergo LTP-IE, preventing specific trajectory replay. Acetylcholine interacts with Kv1.2 channels hypothesized to underlie LTP-IE, and hippocampus receives state-dependent cholinergic input. Excitability changes in dentate gyrus decay after two hours. Regulation of excitability changes would be important for preventing pathological dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C128 discuss model limitations and potential regulatory mechanisms. The logical inference about saturation (C124) is valid. The cited mechanisms for regulation (C125-C126) are appropriate. The speculation about clinical implications (C128) is reasonable and appropriately cautious, referencing the 'blowup' regime observed in simulations.

results.result: While the model assumes homogeneous stochastic gating inputs, real cortical activity contains higher-order structure like grid representations. The model demonstrates replay can occur without additional mnemonic information, but such information would likely increase capacity and robustness. Entorhinal neurons may support persistent activity on LTP-IE timescales.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C131 acknowledge model simplifications regarding gating inputs. The observation about grid cells (C129) is appropriately cited. The conclusion about model sufficiency (C130) is supported by the results. The speculation about persistent activity (C131) is appropriately cited and presented as speculative.

results.result: Empirical replay typically lasts ~100 ms but can last hundreds of milliseconds in larger environments. Replay may be gated by theta oscillations constraining events to 100-200 ms windows. Power-law activity distributions suggest scale-invariance and criticality. The model would not exhibit scale-free patterns due to inhibition, refractoriness, and finite environment size.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C136 discuss replay duration and scale-free dynamics. The experimental observations (C132-C133) are appropriately cited. The discussion of power-law distributions (C134-C135) is supported by citations. The inference about model limitations (C136) is logical given the design constraints.

results.result: The model makes testable predictions: (1) pharmacological blocking of LTP-IE during exploration should prevent replay; (2) inactivating MEC II should inhibit CA3 replay; (3) neurons need not be activated in sequential order during encoding, as ordering is reconstructed from connectivity; (4) replay should follow spatial paths rather than presentation order in virtual reality experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C140 present experimental predictions. The pharmacological prediction (C137) is reasonable and cites appropriate blocking agents. The MEC II prediction (C138) is supported by analogy to cited MEC III results. The core prediction about non-sequential encoding (C139-C140) directly follows from the model mechanism and would be a strong test.

results.result: The model links isotropic spatial connectivity to bidirectional replay, predicting equal probability of forward/reverse replay since LTP-IE stores no directionality. Reverse replay would not be expected for non-spatial sequences. The gating signal may control state-dependent replay occurrence, ensuring replay happens at appropriate times without interfering with other computations.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C145 discuss computational insights. The link between isotropy and bidirectionality (C141-C142) is a logical consequence of the model design. The prediction about non-spatial sequences (C143) follows from the mechanism. The speculation about gating signal function (C144-C145) is reasonable and appropriately cited regarding pattern separation.

results.result: While LTP-IE has only been observed in hippocampus, similar mechanisms may exist in cortex. LTP-IE-like phenomena and preferential connectivity among similarly tuned cells have been observed in cortex. History-dependent excitability changes may occur over multiple timescales. Optogenetically imprinted ensembles might arise via excitability changes rather than Hebbian plasticity. Excitability changes alone might rapidly reshape network dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C29, C100-C106 discuss potential cortical mechanisms and broader implications. While cortical LTP-IE-like phenomena (C101) and preferential connectivity (C102) are cited, the speculation about cortical mechanisms (C29) and reinterpretation of optogenetic results (C105) are presented as possibilities rather than demonstrated facts. The general conclusion (C106) is supported by the hippocampal model but extrapolation to cortex remains speculative.

results.result: The binding pool model could potentially be recast in terms of excitability-based information flow. Persistent spiking's role in working memory is being reevaluated and could theoretically be replaced by excitability increases. The switchboard architecture may suit novel mapping storage. External modulatory inputs can control computation speed in recurrent networks. Excitability-based control without connectivity changes may be a rich framework for studying cognitive flexibility.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C150 discuss broader implications and connections to other work. The comparison to binding pool model (C146) is appropriately cited. The discussion of persistent activity alternatives (C147) cites relevant reevaluation. The inference about novel mappings (C148) is supported by the demonstrated flexibility. The citation about computation speed control (C149) is appropriate. The concluding proposal (C150) is a reasonable synthesis presented as a suggestion for future work.
